title: Lasagne alla Bolognese
subtitle: Classic meat lasagne with slow-cooked ragù and béchamel
excerpt: Lasagne alla bolognese is the canonical Italian layered pasta: slow-cooked beef and pork ragù alternated with béchamel and sheets of pasta, finished with Parmesan and baked until the top is golden and set. It takes time but most of it is unsupervised, and nothing made in a home kitchen is more satisfying to pull out of the oven.
sourceNotes: Lasagne al forno from Emilia-Romagna is one of Italy's most celebrated baked pasta dishes. The definitive recipe was registered with the Bologna Chamber of Commerce in 1982. Artusi, La scienza in cucina e l'arte di mangiar bene (1891), public domain, documents layered pasta bakes from the same tradition. The standard preparation uses beef and pork ragù, béchamel, Parmigiano-Reggiano, and fresh egg pasta.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely, slice into portions, and freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat from frozen at 180°C covered with foil for 45 minutes, removing the foil for the last 10 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Fully assembled lasagne keeps in the fridge for 2 days unbaked. Bring to room temperature for 30 minutes before baking. The ragù can be made 3 days ahead and refrigerated.

glossaryTerms.definition: An Italian meat sauce cooked low and slow until the meat breaks down and the fat merges with the tomato base. The process takes at least 90 minutes; shorter cooking produces a different dish.
A French white sauce made by cooking butter and flour together into a roux, then adding milk gradually and stirring until thick. One of the five French mother sauces.

content.text: Lasagne alla bolognese uses three components: a long-cooked beef and pork

, and lasagne sheets layered in a baking dish. The ragù needs at least 90 minutes of gentle simmering to develop depth; the béchamel and assembly take about 30 minutes. Between them they produce a dish that improves over 2 to 3 days in the fridge and freezes exceptionally well.

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large heavy-based saucepan over a medium heat. Add the {{pancetta}} of diced pancetta and cook for 3 minutes until the fat renders. Add {{onion}} of onion, {{carrot}} of carrot, and {{celery}} of celery. Cook for 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden.

Increase the heat to high. Add {{beef-mince}} of beef mince and {{pork-mince}} of pork mince in batches, breaking up with a spoon and cooking until the meat is brown and any liquid has evaporated. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and {{tomato-puree}} of tomato puree and cook for 2 minutes.

Pour in {{red-wine}} of red wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes. Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} of tinned tomatoes, {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, {{bay-leaves}} of bay leaves, and {{salt-table}} of salt. Stir, reduce the heat to the lowest setting, cover partially, and cook for 90 minutes, stirring every 20 minutes. The ragù should be thick and dark by the end. Remove the bay leaves.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a medium saucepan. Add {{plain-flour}} of flour and stir over a medium heat for 2 minutes until pale and biscuity. Remove from the heat and whisk in the {{whole-milk}} of warm milk a ladleful at a time, returning to the heat between additions and whisking until smooth. Once all the milk is in, stir over a medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes until the sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon. Season with {{nutmeg}} of nutmeg and a pinch of salt.

Heat the oven to 190°C (fan 170°C / gas mark 5). Spread a thin layer of béchamel on the base of a large baking dish (about 30 x 23 cm). Lay {{lasagne-sheets}} of lasagne sheets in a single layer. Spread a third of the ragù over the sheets, then a quarter of the remaining béchamel. Scatter a little {{parmesan}} of Parmesan over. Repeat three more times, finishing with a layer of béchamel and the remaining Parmesan on top.

Cover loosely with foil and bake for 30 minutes. Remove the foil and bake for a further 20 to 25 minutes until the top is golden and bubbling at the edges. Rest for 15 minutes before cutting. The lasagne will firm up as it rests and cut cleanly.

items.symptom: The lasagne sheets are still hard after baking
items.cause: The sheets were not submerged in enough sauce, or the oven temperature was too low.
items.fix: Dried no-cook sheets need to be completely surrounded by moist sauce. If the ragù looks dry before assembling, add a splash of water or stock. Cover the dish tightly with foil for the first 30 minutes.

items.symptom: The lasagne is watery when served
items.cause: The ragù had too much liquid, or the dish was not rested.
items.fix: Reduce the ragù until it is thick before assembling. Always rest the lasagne for 15 minutes after removing from the oven; it sets as it cools.

items.symptom: The top layer is brown but the inside is cold
items.cause: The oven was too hot, or the dish was assembled from cold.
items.fix: If baking from the fridge, add 15 minutes covered with foil at the start. Keep the oven at 190°C rather than hotter.

content.text: Lasagne alla bolognese is the signature dish of Emilia-Romagna, the region that also gave the world Parmigiano-Reggiano, prosciutto di Parma, and tagliatelle al ragù. Bolognese refers to Bologna, the regional capital. In 1982 a recipe was registered with the Chamber of Commerce in Bologna, setting down the standard: green pasta, beef ragù, béchamel, and Parmesan. The home version is slightly looser and dried pasta works well. The British and American layered pasta with meat sauce is related but is a different dish.
